title: Aquatic food production and trade reach new highs while resource health, equity, livelihoods, and value-chain resilience remain contested
source_unit: Food and Agriculture Organization, The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2026: Blue Transformation, Turning Vision into Impact
geography: Global marine and inland fisheries, aquaculture, aquatic-food trade, resources, livelihoods, and regional food systems

denominator.unit: global fisheries and aquaculture production frame

aquaculture_production.unit: million-plus tonnes of aquatic animal production from aquaculture in 2024

production_direction.value: global fisheries and aquaculture production reached a new high

transformation_goal.value: Blue Transformation emphasizes sustainable development of aquaculture, fisheries, and aquatic value chains

resource_condition.value: the report assesses the state and health of marine fishery resources

observations.method: FAO global fisheries and aquaculture statistics, resource assessment, sector analysis, and case-based synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: Production totals and resource assessments aggregate diverse species, systems, and regions; they do not establish sustainability or livelihood improvement for every fishery or producer.
observations.subgroup: Fishers, aquaculture producers, aquatic-food workers, coastal and inland communities, consumers, resource managers, and food-system firms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher production can improve food availability and livelihoods if resource management, labor conditions, and distribution keep ecological and social costs from rising with output.

trade_value.unit: billion US dollars in aquatic animal product trade

trade_direction.value: trade in aquatic animal products continues to reach record levels

market_channel.value: processing, storage, transportation, logistics, trade policies, tariffs, non-tariff measures, and export restrictions shape flows from production to consumption

regional_route.value: aquatic-food trade connects production and consumption across regions

observations.method: FAO trade statistics and analysis of aquatic-food value chains, market access, logistics, and policy conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Trade value does not measure who captures margins, local affordability, labor quality, or ecological costs; flows can change with prices, tariffs, and shocks.
observations.subgroup: Exporting and importing countries, fishers, processors, retailers, consumers, port communities, and workers in cold-chain and logistics systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trade diversification and better logistics can widen access and income, while local procurement and social protection can reduce dependence on volatile export markets.

animal_protein_share.unit: percent of per-capita animal-protein consumption supplied by aquatic animal products

food_security_role.value: aquatic food systems contribute to food security and nutrition as well as livelihoods and sustainable development

access_difference.value: the nutrition contribution of aquatic foods varies with affordability, geography, culture, infrastructure, and distribution

health_boundary.value: sector production and per-capita averages do not show whether particular households can access, afford, or safely consume nutritious aquatic foods

observations.method: FAO food-balance, production, trade, and aquatic-food system analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Per-capita averages conceal within-country inequality, dietary substitution, local prices, preparation, contamination risk, and intra-household allocation.
observations.subgroup: Coastal and inland consumers, low-income households, children, fish-dependent communities, producers, and food-insecure populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local and small-scale aquatic food systems can support nutrition and cultural food practices even where export-oriented growth does not improve local affordability.

denominator.unit: global aquatic-food sustainability and governance frame

core_tension.value: sustainable and equitable growth of marine and inland ecosystems remains a key challenge despite production and trade gains

solution_channels.value: innovation, science, responsible management, and community engagement are identified as pathways for Blue Transformation

resilience.value: resilient and efficient value chains are part of the report's route to more inclusive aquatic food systems

governance_scope.value: resource managers, communities, institutions, industry, producers, and civil society all appear in the transformation frame

observations.method: FAO sustainability, resource-management, value-chain, innovation, and community-governance synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies pathways and examples rather than a universal causal estimate; implementation capacity and power distribution differ across fisheries and aquaculture systems.
observations.subgroup: Small-scale fishers, aquaculture workers, coastal communities, Indigenous and local resource users, regulators, industry, and civil society.
observations.counterinterpretation: Community engagement can improve legitimacy and stewardship, but participation without control over access, prices, safety, or resource decisions may not produce equitable outcomes.

related_sources.claim: FAO FishStat provides complementary global and regional fisheries and aquaculture statistics.
FAO GLOBEFISH provides complementary trade, market, and value-chain context for SOFIA 2026.

boundary: This record adds an aquatic-food, fisheries, aquaculture, nutrition, trade, livelihoods, ecological-resource, and community-governance route. It uses FAO aggregate sector statistics and report synthesis, not respondent-level data, individual fisher histories, household seafood diaries, causal price estimates, or proof that production and trade growth are automatically sustainable or equitable.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official FAO SOFIA 2026 publication and FAO newsroom material reviewed for production highs, aquaculture above 100 million tonnes in 2024, aquatic-food trade value, nutrition contribution, resource-health scope, Blue Transformation, resilient value chains, and equity/community framing.
